headlines.summary: Technology stocks tumbled Tuesday as a sell-off in U.S. semiconductor shares spilled into Asian and European markets.
headlines.article_text: Micron, SK Hynix, Samsung Electronics, ASML shares: tech stocks fall Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Technology stocks tumbled Tuesday as a sell-off in U.S. semiconductor shares spilled into Asian and European markets. China's ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT, reported progress on a new chip structure, intensifying chip competition. Intel and Broadcom CEOs have warned that access to capital could emerge as a major headwind to the artificial intelligence boom. In this article 9984.T-JP ASML STM IFX-DE SKHY Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Samuel Boivin | Nurphoto | Getty Images Technology stocks fell Tuesday, extending a sell-off sparked by worries over artificial intelligence financing and intensifying competition. Memory chip giant Micron was down around 3% in U.S. premarket trading, with other names like Broadcom under pressure. Other memory-related stocks such as SanDisk , Seagate and Western Digital were all around 3% lower. The slide, which follows declines on Wall Street on Monday, comes as investors assessed intensifying competition from China's ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT . Micron shares year-to-date. Over the weekend , CXMT announced significant progress in developing a new chip architecture, designed to increase memory density by packing more data into a smaller space. CXMT is China's leading rival to the likes of Micron and South Korean heavyweights SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics. Analysts broadly see CXMT as trailing the U.S. and South Korean memory leaders, which means any advancement from the Chinese firm could add more competition to the market leaders. "Investors are jittery and looking for excuses to take profit on AI-related stocks that have outperformed this year, especially memory stocks," said UBP's senior equity advisor Vey-Sern Ling. "In reality, while the Chinese memory makers can potentially become a threat to global demand-supply balance over time, in the short run they continue to face technology hurdles, especially for more advanced memory like HBM," Ling told CNBC via email. CXMT shares closed 2.8% lower in Shanghai. Global tech stocks slump Adding fuel to the sell-off was a post by Tesla and SpaceX boss Elon Musk, who said China has the ability to scale production once it figures out how to manufacture something. "When China figures out how to manufacture a product, their ability to scale is often greater than the rest of the world combined," Musk said on Monday. European chip stocks also sank in early morning trade, with semiconductor equipment maker ASML down 3.3%, and STMicroelectronics and German chip maker Infineon both down 5%. Dutch firms BE Semiconductor and ASM International were both around 4% lower at the open. Shares of South Korean chip giant SK Hynix, a leading supplier of high-bandwidth memory chips used in artificial intelligence applications, plunged more than 10%, while rival Samsung Electronics shed 7.4% — both hitting their lowest levels since August. SK Hynix's U.S.-listed stock was down around 5% in premarket trading. watch now VIDEO 4:30 04:30 Tech shakedown spreads as U.S. heavyweights face fresh selling Squawk Box Europe In Japan, shares of tech-focused investment giant SoftBank Group sank 8.5%. The group, which has significant exposure to the global AI industry through its huge investment in OpenAI, led a broader retreat in Japanese semiconductor and electronics shares. Tokyo Electron , a major supplier of chipmaking equipment, dropped 7.2%, while Advantest , which makes semiconductor testing equipment, declined 2.9%. Other Japanese technology stocks also came under pressure. Lasertec fell over 5%, Disco lost 4.7% and Renesas Electronics shed 5.9%. The declines followed a weak session for technology stocks on Wall Street, where the Nasdaq Composite dropped 0.44% on Monday. U.S. memory chipmaker Micron Technology slid 3.9% as 'Vulnerable' AI sentiment? Phillip Wool, chief market strategist at Rayliant Global Advisors, said CXMT's breakthrough marked a significant milestone for Chinese chipmakers , demonstrating their ability to overcome technology restrictions and potentially challenge established players sooner than expected. But he cautioned that the market reaction appeared disproportionate to the immediate competitive threat, given that CXMT has yet to demonstrate large-scale production and continues to lag Samsung and SK Hynix in market share. "More importantly, we're not even talking about HBM here, and the Korean chipmakers are still unquestionably dominating that space, with very little threat at all from the likes of CXMT or anyone else for the foreseeable future," Wool said. He said the sharp sell-off reflected broader anxiety over the AI trade rather than a fundamental shift in the competitive landscape. "I read that more as a sign of how vulnerable AI sentiment is at this moment," Wool said, warning that volatility could persist as investors reassess chip demand and how long semiconductor manufacturers can sustain their pricing power. The chief executives of Intel and Broadcom have warned that access to capital could emerge as a major headwind to the AI boom, even as demand for computing infrastructure continues to outstrip supply. Investors are also looking ahead to a busy week of corporate earnings and U.S. inflation data, which could provide fresh clues on the outlook for interest rates that often have an inverse correlation with growth stocks. headlines.article_text: Visa gets Beijing's green light for bank card business after 40 years of working with China Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Visa said Tuesday it received China's approval to begin the process of establishing a local bank card clearing business. Mastercard and American Express have already gotten the approvals in the last several years. Visa's CEO became chair of the U.S.-China Business Council in June. In this article V Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Dado Ruvic | Reuters BEIJING — U.S. credit card giant Visa announced Tuesday it had received approval from the People's Bank of China for setting up a bank card clearing business in the country. The news comes as the U.S. and Chinese presidents plan for their third meeting this year. "This marks an important milestone toward the company serving China's domestic payments market," Visa said in a statement. "For more than 40 years, Visa has been an active contributor to China's dynamic payments landscape," Visa CEO Ryan McInerney said. "We look forward to taking the necessary steps in the process, pursuant to the PBOC's regulations, to begin operating domestically in China." McInerney joined U.S. President Donald Trump's business delegation to Beijing in May and subsequently became chair of the U.S.-China Business Council in June. The Visa CEO also led a trip to Beijing in early September . "The timing is notable," said George Chen, partner and chair of digital practice, The Asia Group. "Beijing chose to approve visa's license just ahead of the APEC Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen next month, where Xi [Jinping] and Trump are expected to meet again," he said. "The move suggests that Beijing is keen to demonstrate tangible progress for American businesses before Trump's next visit to China." Trump told Fox News after his Beijing trip in May that he brought up Visa's request to gain China market access. After the summit in September, China said it would approve applications from all foreign financial institutions to operate in the country . Entering a closed market Mainland China has kept a tight grip on its financial sector, favoring domestic players and restricting cross-border capital flows. Visa previously said it had applied with the PBOC in May 2020 to operate a bank card clearing institution. The company has worked with Chinese banks for dual-branded cards, for which China's UnionPay processes transactions domestically and Visa processes overseas payments. In January, Visa said the mainland China-issued cards could be linked to Apple Pay for use overseas. Rival Mastercard 's joint venture in China said it started processing payments in 2024 after getting the PBOC's approval to begin bank card clearing preparations in February 2020. American Express was the first, receiving its processing license in June 2020 after getting the PBOC nod back in 2018 . Mobile pay dominates daily consumer transactions in China, primarily facilitated by Tencent's WeChat and Alibaba-affiliate Ant's Alipay.
